steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our EnduRL paper on mixed traffic control with robot vehicles. It should motivate the problem from congestion and the gap between simulated car-following (IDM) and real-world driving, introduce EnduRL and our RL-based robot vehicle, and summarize the experiments and results.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Congestion and its causes (asymmetric driving theory)
2. Mixed traffic control with robot vehicles; prior strategies, mostly in simulation
3. Problem: simulated car-following (IDM) is too timid vs real-world data
4. Limited prior fixes; EnduRL and our RL-based RV
5. Experiments, metrics, results, code

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Congestion and its causes
- every major city: congestion; bridge bottlenecks, phantom jams on highways
- unsteady flow -> more travel time, energy consumption, collision risk
- causes not fully understood; prominent explanation: asymmetric driving theory
- human driving: frequent under-/over-reactions; heterogeneous styles, differences in estimation, reaction, actuation times
- intensify in dense traffic -> congestion

2. Mixed traffic control
- more vehicles with varying autonomy -> mixed traffic control: Robot Vehicles (RVs) address perturbations from Human-driven Vehicles (HVs)
- strategies: heuristics, longitudinal dynamics models, machine learning
- effective at intersections, highways, bottlenecks, large networks; RV penetration as low as 5\%
- mostly simulation, e.g. Simulation of Urban MObility (SUMO); model-based methods for HV car-following

3. Simulated car-following too timid
- Intelligent Driver Model (IDM): popular, minimal parameters
- stochasticity added; imperfections in perception, processing, actuation
- still constrained: 92\% of stochastic IDM accelerations (default params) in [-0.5,0.5]~m/s^{2}
- real world (I- 24 MOTION dataset): only 68\% in same range -> \mathbf{24\%} difference
- real-world long tail up to [-3,3]~m/s^{2}
- simulation = safe/timid; missing aggressive behaviors (sudden braking, rapid acceleration)
- RVs validated only with timid behavior may struggle with real-world perturbations -> safety, stability, efficiency goals

4. Prior fixes and EnduRL
- limited research bridging IDM and real-world driving
- enhancements: random noise, calibration with real data
- fall short: full variability; restrictive assumptions, artificial constraints
- EnduRL: periodically sample accelerations from real-world dataset during car-following -> more variability, aggressive accel/decel
- RL-based RV: downstream traffic info -> forecast congestion stages, preemptive actions

5. Experiments and results
- compare with prior RVs; Ring and Bottleneck (Fig. 1); 1500+ simulation runs
- safety: time to collision (TTC), deceleration rate to avoid a crash (DRAC)
- efficiency: fuel economy, throughput; stability: acceleration variation, wave attenuation
- widely adopted metrics
- Ring: safety and efficiency up to \mathbf{54}\%, stability up to \mathbf{97}\%
- Bottleneck: safety \mathbf{66}\%, efficiency \mathbf{41}\%, stability \mathbf{34}\%
- among few studies addressing sim vs real gap
- code: https://github.com/poudel-bibek/EnduRL

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Traffic congestion is a problem in every major city in the world. It can come from bottlenecks caused by infrastructure like bridges, or from more subtle things like phantom jams on highways. When traffic flow is unsteady during congestion, travel time, energy consumption and collision risk all go up. The causes of congestion are not fully understood, but one prominent explanation is the asymmetric driving theory. According to this theory human driving has frequent under- and over-reactions, which come from heterogeneous driving styles and from individual differences in estimation, reaction, and actuation times. In dense traffic these factors get stronger and eventually they lead to congestion.

More and more vehicles with different levels of autonomy are coming into our transportation system, and so the idea of mixed traffic control has emerged, which means using Robot Vehicles (RVs) to deal with the perturbations that Human-driven Vehicles (HVs) produce and amplify. Different control strategies have been introduced, for example ones based on heuristics, on models of longitudinal dynamics, and on machine learning. These techniques have been shown to reduce congestion in scenarios like intersections, highways, bottlenecks, and large networks, with RV penetration rates as low as 5\%. Most of these studies are done in simulation with software like Simulation of Urban MObility (SUMO), and there model-based methods are mostly used to represent the car-following behaviors of HVs.

There are many car-following models for longitudinal control of a vehicle, and the Intelligent Driver Model (IDM) is a popular one with minimal parameters. Stochasticity is often added to the model to simulate heterogeneous driving behaviors that reflect individual differences between drivers, and the simulation also accounts for imperfections in perception, processing, and actuation. But even with these adjustments the car-following behaviors of HVs are very constrained: 92\% of the accelerations from the stochastic IDM model with default parameters are within the range [-0.5,0.5]~m/s^{2}. But only 68\% of real-world accelerations (taken from the I- 24 MOTION dataset) are in that range, so there is a \mathbf{24\%} difference. Also real-world accelerations have a long tail that goes up to [-3,3]~m/s^{2}. This shows that simulated car-following mostly shows safe or timid behaviors, and does not represent the more aggressive real-world behaviors like sudden braking and rapid accelerations. So RVs that were developed and validated for improving traffic with only timid driving behaviors may have trouble handling real-world perturbations, and this makes them less effective at the goals of safety, stability, and efficiency

Not much research so far bridges the gap between IDM and real-world driving. Some enhancements to IDM have been proposed to make simulation more accurate, like adding random noise and calibrating with real-world driving data. But they do not capture the full variability of traffic and are often not broadly applicable because they have restrictive assumptions and artificial constraints on how vehicles behave. We introduce EnduRL, a framework that overcomes these limitations by periodically sampling accelerations from the real-world dataset during car-following. This gives more variability in driving behavior with more aggressive accelerations and decelerations. We also propose a reinforcement learning (RL)-based RV that uses downstream traffic information to forecast congestion stages and take preemptive actions to improve traffic conditions.

We compare EnduRL with RVs from prior studies in comprehensive experiments in two mixed traffic environments, Ring and Bottleneck (see Fig. 1), with 1500+ simulation runs. For safety we use two surrogate measures, time to collision (TTC) and deceleration rate to avoid a crash (DRAC). For efficiency we measure fuel economy and throughput, and for stability we measure acceleration variation and wave attenuation. These metrics are widely used in traffic engineering. The results show that in Ring our RV improves safety and efficiency by up to \mathbf{54}\%, and stability by up to \mathbf{97}\%. In Bottleneck our RV improves safety by up to \mathbf{66}\%, efficiency up to \mathbf{41}\%, and stability up to \mathbf{34}\%. As far as we know, EnduRL is one of the few studies that address the important gap between car-following behaviors in simulation and in the real world, and it significantly improves the safety, stability, and efficiency of mixed traffic compared to previous studies. The project code is in the repository: https://github.com/poudel-bibek/EnduRL

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Every major city in the world faces traffic congestion, from infrastructure-induced bottlenecks on bridges to more subtle phenomena like phantom jams on highways. Unsteady traffic flow during congestion increases travel time, energy consumption, and collision risk [1]. While the causes of congestion are not fully understood, a prominent explanation for congestion is the asymmetric driving theory [2]. This theory posits that human driving is characterized by frequent under- and over-reactions, which stem from heterogeneous driving styles and individual differences in estimation, reaction, and actuation times. These factors intensify in dense traffic and eventually lead to congestion [3].

As more vehicles with varying levels of autonomy enter our transportation system, the concept of mixed traffic control, i.e., using Robot Vehicles (RVs) to address perturbations produced and amplified by Human-driven Vehicles (HVs), has emerged [4,5,6,7]. Various control strategies have been introduced, such as those based on heuristics [8], models of longitudinal dynamics [9,10], and machine learning [11]. These techniques have proven effective in reducing congestion in scenarios such as intersections [12], highways [13], bottlenecks [14], and large networks [15] at RV penetration rates as low as 5\%. Most of these studies are carried out in simulation using software such as Simulation of Urban MObility (SUMO) [16], where model-based methods dominate in representing the car-following behaviors of HVs [17,18].

Among the various car-following models that enable longitudinal control of a vehicle, the Intelligent Driver Model (IDM) [19] is a popular choice with minimal parameters. To simulate heterogeneous driving behaviors that account for drivers' individual differences, stochasticity is often integrated with the model, and imperfections in perception, processing, and actuation are accounted for in the simulation [20]. However, even with these adjustments, the car-following behaviors of HVs are largely constrained: 92\% of the accelerations derived using the stochastic IDM model with the default parameters [17] lie within the range [-0.5,0.5]~m/s^{2}. In contrast, only 68\% of real-world accelerations (extracted from the I- 24 MOTION dataset [21]) fall within the same range, a \mathbf{24\%} difference. Further, real-world accelerations have a long tail extending up to [-3,3]~m/s^{2}. This reveals that simulated car-following mainly depicts safe or timid behaviors and lacks representation of more aggressive real-world behaviors such as sudden braking and rapid accelerations [22,23]. Consequently, RVs developed and validated with only timid driving behaviors may struggle to handle real-world perturbations, impeding their effectiveness in achieving the goals of safety, stability, and efficiency

Limited research to date bridges the gap between IDM and real-world driving [24]. Enhancements to IDM, such as integrating random noise and calibrating with real-world driving data, have been proposed to improve simulation accuracy. However, they fall short of capturing the full traffic variability and often lack broad applicability because of restrictive assumptions and artificial constraints on vehicle behaviors [25,26,27,28,29,30]. We introduce EnduRL, a framework that overcomes these limitations by periodically sampling accelerations from the real-world dataset during car-following. This produces more variability in driving behavior, with more aggressive accelerations and decelerations. In addition, we propose a reinforcement learning (RL)-based RV that uses downstream traffic information to forecast congestion stages and take preemptive actions to improve traffic conditions.

We compare EnduRL with RVs developed in prior studies through comprehensive experiments in two mixed traffic environments, Ring [31] and Bottleneck [14] (see Fig. 1), over 1500+ simulation runs. To evaluate safety, we use two surrogate measures, time to collision (TTC) and deceleration rate to avoid a crash (DRAC); for efficiency, we measure fuel economy and throughput; for stability, we measure acceleration variation and wave attenuation. These metrics are widely adopted in traffic engineering [32,33,10]. Our results show that in Ring, our RV improves both safety and efficiency by up to \mathbf{54}\% and stability by up to \mathbf{97}\%, whereas in Bottleneck, it improves safety by up to \mathbf{66}\%, efficiency by up to \mathbf{41}\%, and stability by up to \mathbf{34}\%. To the best of our knowledge, EnduRL is among the few studies that address the crucial gap between car-following behaviors in simulation and in the real world, and it significantly improves the safety, stability, and efficiency of mixed traffic compared to previous studies. The project code can be found in the repository: https://github.com/poudel-bibek/EnduRL

References:
[1] Colin Buchanan. Traffic in Towns: A study of the long term problems of traffic in urban areas . Routledge, 2015.
[2] Hwasoo Yeo. Asymmetric microscopic driving behavior theory . University of California, Berkeley, 2008.
[3] Hwasoo Yeo and Alexander Skabardonis. Understanding stop-and-go traffic in view of asymmetric traffic theory. In Transportation and Traffic Theory 2009: Golden Jubilee: Papers selected for presentation at ISTTT18, a peer reviewed series since 1959 , pages 99–115. Springer, 2009.
[4] Xuan Di and Rongye Shi. A survey on autonomous vehicle control in the era of mixed-autonomy: From physics-based to ai-guided driving policy learning. Transportation research part C: emerging technologies , 125:103008, 2021.
